title: Writing Across Genres
keyIdea: Each form of writing has conventions: the layout and features its readers expect. A script uses speaker names, colons and stage directions in brackets, with no speech marks. A formal letter follows a set layout, from the addresses and date to a salutation, paragraphs and a sign-off that matches the greeting. Notes for a talk are short prompts, not full sentences. A poem uses lineation, so where each line ends matters. Choosing the right form, register and conventions makes a piece work for its purpose and audience.

kid: A genre or form is a kind of writing: a story, a script, a poem, a letter, notes for a talk. Each form has conventions. These are the rules of layout and style that readers expect. You can often name the form from its shape before you read a word.

A formal letter has a set layout. Your address and the date go at the top right. The reader's name and address go on the left. Then comes the salutation, the greeting. If you write "Dear Sir or Madam", you sign off "Yours faithfully". If you use their name, as in "Dear Ms Patel", you sign off "Yours sincerely". The register is formal: full sentences and no slang.

A script shows speech in a different way from a story. Each line starts with the speaker's name and a colon. There are no speech marks and no "he said". How a line is spoken, and what people do, goes in brackets as stage directions.

Notes for a talk are short bullet points you glance at, so you can look up at your audience. A poem is set out in lines. Where each line ends is called lineation. A line usually ends best on a strong word, like a noun or a verb, not on "the" or "of".
adult: The Key Stage 3 English programme of study asks pupils to write for a wide range of purposes and audiences. This includes stories, scripts and poetry, notes and talks, and personal and formal letters. They should also draw on what they read to choose the right form and register. In the US, Common Core W.6.4 to W.8.4 ask for writing whose organisation and style suit the task, purpose and audience. Lesson 470 covers choosing a form and tone for a purpose; this lesson goes one step further into the conventions of each form.

Useful terms: form or genre is the kind of text. Conventions are the layout and language features readers expect. Register is the level of formality. Salutation and sign-off are the greeting and closing of a letter. Stage directions are the bracketed instructions in a script, and lineation is how a poem is divided into lines, which may be grouped into stanzas. UK letters pair "Dear Sir or Madam" with "Yours faithfully" and a named greeting with "Yours sincerely"; US letters usually end with "Sincerely" in both cases.

Common mistakes to watch for: keeping speech marks and "he said" in a script; pairing "Dear Sir or Madam" with "Yours sincerely"; writing out a whole talk word for word and reading it aloud; and chopping prose into random lines and calling it a poem. A careful writer checks each convention against a model text before handing work in.

In the lab, learners name four fragments from their conventions and build a formal letter in the right order. They match salutations to sign-offs, then turn a prose extract into a script one change at a time. Last, they break a sentence into four lines of poetry that end on strong words. The Challenge mixes these, with feedback on each wrong answer.

visual.caption: Which form is the feature from? Drag each one into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name forms from their conventions, build a formal letter, match sign-offs, turn prose into a script and break a sentence into lines of poetry.

practice.prompt: A letter begins "Dear Sir or Madam". Which sign-off matches?
practice.hint: Do you know the reader's name? Which sign-off goes with an unknown name?
practice.explain: With "Dear Sir or Madam" the name is not known, so a UK formal letter ends "Yours faithfully".

practice.prompt: A script has {a} lines for Maya and {b} lines for Tom. How many speaker names will appear on the left?
practice.hint: Every line of a script starts with a speaker name. Add Maya's {a} lines and Tom's {b}.
practice.explain: Each line starts with its speaker's name, so {a} + {b} = {=a+b} names appear.

practice.prompt: A poem has {s} stanzas, each with {n} lines. How many lines is that?
practice.hint: A stanza is a group of lines. Multiply the stanzas by the lines in each one.
practice.explain: {s} stanzas of {n} lines make {=s*n} lines in all.

practice.prompt: Which line is written as a script?
choices: Tom said quietly that he thought so.
practice.hint: Look for a speaker name, a colon and brackets.
practice.explain: A script line starts with the speaker name and a colon, and puts how it is said in brackets.

pool.prompt: In a UK formal letter, where does your own address go?
choices: Top right, with the date below
At the bottom, after your name
pool.hint: It is the first thing on the page, on the opposite side to the reader's address.
pool.explain: Your address goes top right, with the date beneath it. The reader's address goes on the left.

pool.prompt: Which is the best set of notes for a talk?
choices: • Hook: a question • Point 1: cost • End: ask for questions
A full page of sentences to read out
One long paragraph with no breaks
pool.hint: You need to glance at notes and look up at the audience.
pool.explain: Short bullet prompts let you glance down and keep eye contact. A full page tempts you to read it out.

pool.prompt: Which split into lines works best for a poem?
choices: The rain keeps drumming / on the roof of the bus
The rain keeps drumming on the / roof of the bus
The rain keeps / drumming on the roof of / the bus
pool.hint: Look at the last word of each line. Is it strong or small?
pool.explain: Ending on "drumming" and "bus" gives each line a strong last word. Ending on "the" or "of" leaves lines hanging.

pool.prompt: You change a story extract into a script. What do you take out?
pool.hint: Which features belong to stories, not scripts?
pool.explain: Scripts drop speech marks and reporting clauses like "he said"; the speaker name shows who talks.

pool.prompt: A talk has {p} main points. Each needs 1 bullet, and you add 1 bullet for the hook and 1 for the ending. How many bullets?
pool.hint: Count one bullet per main point, then add the hook and the ending.
pool.explain: {p} point bullets plus a hook and an ending make {=p+2} bullets.

pool.prompt: A poem has {s} stanzas of {k} lines. You add one more stanza of {k} lines. How many lines now?
pool.hint: Find the lines in {s} stanzas first, then add {k} more for the new stanza.
pool.explain: {s} stanzas of {k} lines is {=s*k} lines. One more stanza adds {k}, making {=s*k+k}.

pool.prompt: A letter starts "Dear Mr Khan". Which sign-off matches?
pool.hint: You know the reader's name. Which sign-off goes with a named greeting?
pool.explain: A named greeting, "Dear Mr Khan", pairs with "Yours sincerely" in a UK formal letter.

pool.prompt: Which sentence suits the register of a formal letter of complaint?
choices: I am writing to complain about the late buses on Route 12.
OMG the buses are sooo late lol
pool.hint: Formal register means full sentences and no slang.
pool.explain: A formal letter uses full sentences, standard English and no slang, so the first line fits.
